title: Parish money
hookLine: supporting the parish keeps its doors and its charity open
tomorrow: what do you say when the Church is the one that let you down?

cards: Every streaming service sends a monthly bill. Nobody bills you for the lights in church, the heat in winter, the food pantry, the roof. Somebody pays.
In the Acts of the Apostles, the first believers in Jerusalem sold what they had and laid the money at the apostles' feet, and it was shared out to each as they had need.
Luke says what came of it: nobody among them was in need. So who keeps the lights on now, and why should anyone care?

teach.b: Paul, gathering money for the poor in Jerusalem, tells the Corinthians how to give: "Every one as he hath determined in his heart, not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
The Church names it among its precepts, the basic duties of Catholics: help provide for the material needs of the Church, each according to their ability. No amount is set.

teach.h: GIFTS WITH THE BREAD AND WINE.
teach.b: And the money doesn't sit outside the Mass; the people's gifts are brought forward with the bread and wine. What it can pay for: the lights and the heat, and also the pantry, help for a family behind on rent, a school.
Keep the doors open, and the charity stays open behind them. A neighbor tradition gives this a central place.
In Islam, zakat, alms given from one's wealth, is a pillar of the faith, and the Qur'an pairs it with prayer, in Pickthall's English: "Establish worship, pay the poor-due."
It even says the ones who tend God's places of worship are those who believe, pray and pay the poor-due.
Shared ground: both treat giving as worship, not a fee, and both tie the house of prayer to the poor.
An honest difference: zakat has a set share and named kinds of recipients; the Catholic precept names no amount, leaving it to each person's means.

how: Catholics support their parish through the Sunday collection and other giving, as each is able; the gifts are brought forward with the bread and wine at the preparation of the gifts.

games.q: your little brother gets his first paycheck and asks if he has to give some to the parish. what fits Paul's line?
o: give what he decides in his heart, gladly, as he's able.
give an exact percentage, or it doesn't count.

games.why: every one as he hath determined in his heart, not with sadness, or of necessity. the Church's precept also names no amount.

practice: Count on your fingers what a parish, or any place people gather, has given you or someone you love: a baptism, a funeral, a meal, a hall for a party, a quiet pew. Go as far as you can.
If you pray, you can give thanks for whoever paid for the lights on those days; if not, just hold the list.

wordCard.voice: Parish money. The giving that keeps a parish's doors, worship and charity open, each according to their means. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a cheerful giver. Paul's phrase in 2 Corinthians 9:7.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the doors open. Gladly, and not of necessity, as Paul put it. Till tomorrow.
